In a preprint paper uploaded to the arXiv repository in July 2025, Marathon scientists had predicted this process could produce roughly 2 tonnes of gold annually for every gigawatt (GW) of thermal fusion power

A San Francisco-based company named Marathon Fusion announced on October 21 that it had ‘converted’ mercury into gold in an experiment in September and that it had achieved a production rate tenfold greater than a record reported by CERN in 2025.

The company has also proposed a programme in which mercury-198 is exposed to high-energy neutrons produced by nuclear fusion — in an existing power plant — converting it into radioactive mercury-197, which subsequently decays into stable gold-197. In a preprint paper uploaded to the arXiv repository in July 2025, Marathon scientists had predicted this process could produce roughly 2 tonnes of gold annually for every gigawatt (GW) of thermal fusion power.

This said, the company has not said if its recent claim has been independently verified — there are no public records indicating that — nor has it disclosed how much gold it actually produced. Overall, there are at least seven caveats around the claims and the hype that has erupted around it.

In nuclear fusion, light nuclei, such as deuterium and tritium, are forced together, releasing high-energy neutrons and energy. The proposal is to have these neutrons strike mercury nuclei and eventually produce gold nuclei. The latter is called nuclear transmutation, not nuclear fusion. Neither the gold nor the mercury nuclei undergo any fusion of their own. Nuclear transmutation is well-known in nuclear physics. In other words the claim about “using” fusion to turn mercury into gold can be misleading.

On its website, Marathon Fusion has published data showing the energy signatures associated with mercury-197 and its decay into gold-197. It is not possible to infer how much gold was produced from this information, nor its purity or how efficiently the process works. Marathon has also not placed a detailed experimental methodology or independent verification in the public domain. Its prior research, described in the preprint paper, was based on computer simulations.

In 2025, CERN had reported that interactions between lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider had produced around 86 billion gold nuclei from 2015 to 2018. This is just around 0.029 billionths of gram — about the amount of gold you can buy with 0.0000414 paise. These nuclei existed for mere fractions of a second before disintegrating further. CERN was also just conducting particle-physics research, not attempting to manufacture gold on a commercial scale. And Marathon Fusion has not explained exactly how it calculated its tenfold improvement.

In the 2025 preprint paper, the authors estimated that a suitable nuclear fusion plant could produce around 2,000 kg of gold every year per gigawatt of thermal power. The figure is rooted in certain advanced computer simulations of neutron transport and nuclear reactions. It is not based on the workings of a functional, commercial reactor. Marathon Fusion has also described plans for a reactor with a fusion power target of just 1 kW, which is one-million-times smaller than 1 GW. Long story short, even if Marathon Fusion’s claimed experiment in September demonstrated converting mercury to gold, it cannot be used to validate the company’s projections of producing gold on an industrial scale.

Only around 10% of the mercury that occurs naturally is mercury-198, which is the isotope Marathon Fusion proposes to use. However, its computer simulations assumed mercury enriched to 90% mercury-198. This will require a programme to enrich mercury isotopes on an industrial scale. Second, mercury is extremely toxic, so the facilities will have to have specialised containment materials and protocols and environmental safeguards. Marathon Fusion has acknowledged these difficulties and has proposed technological solutions but their practicality and costs have yet to be determined at scale.

The Marathon Fusion way to make gold is not implausible but the resulting gold will be radioactive. Other nuclear reactions happening at the same time will also create other radioactive isotopes, including gold-195, which has a half-life of around 186 days. And according to Marathon’s own simulations, the resulting gold mix will need around 6.8 years to meet one low-level radioactive waste threshold, 13.7 years to fall below a specified radioactive material labelling threshold, and 17.7 years to meet a more conservative benchmark. It will be possible to purify the isotopes to reduce these timelines but not without adding to the costs.

The Marathon Fusion website says producing gold in this way could roughly double the revenue of fusion power plants without compromising electricity output. To this end, the preprint paper modelled a 1.5-GW thermal fusion power plant that cost $3 billion to build and which operates at 100% capacity for three decades while converting 40% of its thermal output to electricity. In this scenario the plant will generate around $263 million a year from electricity sold at $50 per megawatt-hour. And producing three tonnes of gold a year and selling it at $100,000 per kilogram would add $300 million in revenue. The problem? Commercial fusion power does not yet exist and these figures are all based on expectations of the future.

articles.title: The other face of air pollution | Excerpt from The Nitrogen Bomb by Jacob Koshy
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The book explores how ammonia, largely emitted by agricultural activities, contributes to worsening air quality across the Indo-Gangetic Plain

The Indo-Gangetic Plain (IGP) stretches across northern India in a 2,500-kilometre arc from Pakistan to Bangladesh and is home to nearly half a billion people. It is one of the most intensively farmed landscapes on earth, and by every atmospheric measure, one of the most chemically burdened places that has been peopled for millennia. What Odén [Svante Odén, the Swedish scientist who first linked acid rain and its wide-ranging environmental harms] mapped in Scandinavia — nitrogen from farms, nitrogen oxides from engines, ammonia reacting with acids to produce particles that choke lungs and kill quietly — is happening here, now, on a scale and at a speed that would make Europe’s post-war industrial peak antediluvian.

In 2025, I reported on a study by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a think tank, that said secondary pollutants, particularly ammonium sulphate that forms when sulphur dioxide from coal plants meets ammonia from fertilised fields, were responsible for nearly one-third of India’s PM2.5 pollution burden.

I remember writing then, trying to explain to readers who, like me, had been led to believe that Delhi’s winters were a problem of primary pollutants from stubble fires and diesel exhaust: ‘Primary pollutants are those that result from the burning of fossil fuels from automobiles, coal plants and organic matter.’ The distinction matters because it changes everything about how you think about solutions. During Delhi’s most polluted winter months, the CREA analysis found, it was secondary pollutants that constituted nearly 41 per cent of all fine particles in the winter air. The problem isn’t what you can see coming out of a tailpipe or a chimney but what is being silently assembled in the atmosphere, molecule by molecule and reaction by reaction.

The one-third figure, however, carries a chemist’s caveat. Professor Srinidhi Balasubramanian, who teaches in the Department of Environmental Science and Engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, has spent close to two decades studying ammonia as an agricultural air pollutant — first in the maize belt of the American Midwest, at the University of Illinois, following it up at the University of Minnesota, and now across the Indo-Gangetic Plain.

She begins her air-quality exposition to me with a line borrowed from a Class VII science textbook. ‘Acid plus base forms a salt,’ she told me. ‘It is as simple as that.’ The acids are the familiar villains — nitrogen oxides from combustion and the sulphur dioxide from coal that is yellowing the Taj Mahal. The base, ‘the single most dominant one, by any stretch’, is ammonia, and the source of that ammonia is overwhelmingly agricultural. Her 2021 work put the farming share at roughly 80 per cent globally, and India, she reckons, at 80 to 85 per cent, the rest leaking from fertiliser plants and industry.

If you look at it, it is the other side of the coin that Odén puzzled over in Scandinavia. The problem he had identified was acids and what she is drawing attention to is the base. ‘This is the other face of acid rain,’ Balasubramanian said. ‘As acid rain reduces, your PM problem exaggerates.’ Where Smith’s Manchester and Odén’s Sweden carried a surplus of acid and watched it fall, the fertilised plains of northern India carry, on top of their acids, an overwhelming surplus of the base — and the salt the two make is settling into human lungs. Her own modelling refines the arithmetic behind the CREA figure: ammonia acting alone accounts for about a quarter of India’s PM2.5, she estimates; bundled with the nitrogen oxides and coal-derived sulphur it reacts with, the inorganic secondary fraction climbs to roughly 40 per cent, and with the organic secondaries added, the national balance tips to something like 45 per cent primary against 55 per cent secondary.

Dr. Balasubramanian is among the small group of Indian scientists who have been tracing the chemistry of what happens over the IGP, across multiple institutions. The foundational work began at the Indian Institute of Technology, Kanpur (IIT-K) with Sachchida Nand Tripathi, who in 2003 established what would become the National Aerosol Facility, the first of its kind in India.

Kanpur is almost the geographic centre of the IGP and from here his group built the long-term datasets on trace gases and aerosol properties that first revealed the seasonal patterns of IGP pollution. A 2014 study from his lab documented four years of continuous measurements of SO2, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, and ozone at Kanpur, establishing the winter loading patterns that make IGP winters chemically unlike any other season anywhere. Cold temperatures push the chemical equilibrium towards the particle phase, and the planetary boundary layer — the lid of air above the city — often compresses below 400 metres, trapping precursor gases until they react. Nitrogen oxides from vehicles and industry peak in winter, the group found, at exactly the moment when the atmospheric conditions for converting them to ammonium nitrate particles are most favourable.

articles.title: J&K Cabinet expansion, swearing-in on October 27
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: National Conference spokesperson Tanvir Sadiq said the party leadership, including Omar Abdullah and party president Farooq Abdullah, will decide on the new faces to be inducted into the Council of Ministers
The expansion of the Jammu and Kashmir Council of Ministers headed by Chief Minister Omar Abdullah will take place in Srinagar on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), party officials said.

"The oath-taking ceremony for the new ministers is scheduled to take place at 10.30 am on Tuesday (October 27, 2026)," National Conference spokesperson Tanvir Sadiq told reporters in Srinagar on Monday (October 26, 2026).
Mr. Sadiq said the party leadership, including Omar Abdullah and party president Farooq Abdullah, will decide on the new faces to be inducted into the Council of Ministers.
"I think by this evening it will be clear as to who all are being sworn in tomorrow," he added.

The Chief Minister on Saturday (October 24, 2026) called on Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha and sought time for swearing in new Ministers as part of reshuffle and expansion in the Council of Ministers.
Asked about the controversial statement regarding Pakistan made by Mr. Farooq Abdullah, the NC spokesperson said that the statement was taken "out of context".

"If you listen to the entire speech, he (Farooq Abdullah) made it clear how the tribal invaders came here and the injustices that emanated from the neighbouring country against Jammu and Kashmir. This is just petty politics being played by the BJP when they take out one part of the speech and present it out of context," he added.

articles.title: Pakistan’s Punjab government extends detention of Imran Khan’s sisters by 30 days
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Dr. Uzma Khan remain in Kot Lakhpat Jail under a public safety law, as PTI leader Moonis Elahi calls the detention “politically motivated”

The Punjab government in Pakistan has extended the detention of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan's three sisters for another 30 days under a public safety law, an official said on Monday (October 26, 2026).
Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Dr. Uzma Khan have been detained at Lahore's Kot Lakhpat Jail for over a month under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960.

While Ms. Aleema was detained on September 20, 2026, Ms. Uzma and Ms. Noreen were taken into custody the following day, amid a crackdown on efforts to mobilise support for the jailed Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder.

An assistant advocate general of Punjab informed the Lahore High Court (LHC) on Monday that the government had extended the detention of Mr. Khan's three sisters for another 30 days, on the recommendation of the Lahore deputy commissioner.
The court subsequently disposed of a petition seeking the trio's release. The petition was filed by Ms. Aleema's son, Shahrez, challenging the detention of the sisters.
Rana Mudassar Umar, counsel for the petitioner, told the court last week that the three sisters remained in jail despite the expiry of the 30-day detention period on October 20, 2026.
Subsequently, Lahore High Court Justice Abher Gul Khan directed the Punjab home secretary and the Kot Lakhpat jail superintendent to appear at the next hearing and submit their replies.

The sisters were detained amid PTI's efforts to organise nationwide protests demanding Mr. Khan's release. The former Prime Minister, 74, has been in jail since August 2023 and faces multiple cases, which he and his party have described as politically motivated.

PTI leaders criticised the Punjab government, led by Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, over the extension of the detention orders, questioning the need to hold the sisters when, they said, they were not wanted in any criminal case.
Former federal minister and PTI leader Moonis Elahi termed the detention illegal, alleging that the government was using preventive detention to target the party and its leadership.

"Preventive detention cannot be used as a substitute for ordinary criminal law. Their detention is politically motivated and part of a wider crackdown on the party and its leadership," he said, calling for the sisters' immediate release.

articles.title: Coimbatore school student’s death case: probe transferred to CB-CID
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Coimbatore city police handed over a copy of the order to family members of the deceased, who along with relatives and members of various political parties have been staging a protest for the past few days, demanding arrest of all persons who abetted the suicide.

Director General of Police Mahesh Kumar Aggarwal transferred the investigation into the alleged death by suicide of Class XI student A. Akilan (16) in Coimbatore to the Crime Bran Criminal Investigation Department (CB-CID) on Monday (October 26, 2026).

The DGP’s order stated that the case, which was registered by the Peelamedu police in Coimbatore under Sections 115(2), 108 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita read with 3(2)(v) of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act in connection with the death on October 22, has been transferred to the CB-CID for further investigation.

The order directed the Coimbatore City Police Commissioner to hand over the original case file and all connected records of the case to the DGP, CB-CID, immediately. The DGP, CB-CID, will nominate an investigating officer, who will take up the investigation.

Personnel from the city police handed over a copy of the order to family members of the deceased, who along with relatives and members of various political parties and organisations have been staging a protest near South Taluk office for the past few days, demanding arrest of all persons who abetted the suicide.

Akilan, who belongs to a Scheduled Caste community, was found dead in his house on October 21. The police arrested two of his classmates , who belong to different dominant castes, two days later for allegedly having subjected him to caste-based harassment. The police were also investigating allegations levelled by Akilan’s mother against a teacher and the headmaster.
(Assistance for overcoming suicidal thoughts is available on the State’s health helpline 104, Tele-MANAS 14416, and Sneha’s suicide prevention helpline 044-24640050.)

articles.title: ‘No understanding of nationalism’: West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari slams TMC
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari accused the previous government of adopting the ‘Joy Bangla’ slogan of Bangladesh; takes a dig at CJP

West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Monday (October 26, 2026) slammed the previous Trinamool Congress government for allegedly indulging in appeasement politics, claiming that it had "no understanding of nationalism" and planned to turn the State into "greater Bangladesh".
Mr. Adhikari also accused the previous government of composing a separate song for the State, designing a flag and adopting the 'Joy Bangla' slogan of the neighbouring country.

Speaking to reporters in Tamluk, West Bengal, after a ' bhoomi pujan ' for a BJP party office, the Chief Minister said, "The previous government in Bengal had no understanding of nationalism, engaged in appeasement politics, and planned to turn the state into greater Bangladesh."
"That is why they had composed a separate song for the state, designed a flag and adopted the 'Joy Bangla' slogan of Bangladesh," he said.
Mr. Adhikari urged the people to remain united and stand with Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Taking a dig at the Cockroach Janta Party for its protests over alleged irregularities in the SIR exercise, the CM appealed to the people to make sure that the ' Dimagi Naxal ', ' tukde tukde ' gangs, cockroaches and termites "do not breed" in Bengal.

articles.title: Congress leader seeks action against Chief Secretaries of six States for skipping PAC hearing
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Absence of officials despite being summoned amounts to breach of privilege, Congress leader and panel chair Venugopal tells Speaker seeking appropriate action

The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) chairperson and senior Congress leader, K.C. Venugopal, has written to Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla seeking action against the Chief Secretaries of six States for not appearing before the panel despite being summoned.

In a letter to the Lok Sabha Speaker dated October 22, Mr. Venugopal flagged the absence of the Chief Secretaries from Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Punjab, Odisha, Bihar and Madhya Pradesh at a hearing on irregularities in scholarship schemes for students belonging to Scheduled Castes.

The Congress leader noted that the panel, which was examining pre-matric and post-matric scholarship programmes for students belonging to Scheduled Castes, had found delays in onboarding States on the national scholarship portal, gaps in coordination between the Centre and States, and problems in disbursement of funds during a study visit to Jaipur in September. Communications went to the six States on October 8 and 9, asking Chief Secretaries and officials of the departments concerned to appear before the PAC in connection with the irregularities, Mr. Venugopal said in the letter.

However, none of the six Chief Secretaries turned up at the meeting, though exemptions were not granted, he noted. Secretaries of the Social Welfare Departments of Karnataka and Punjab and the Education Secretary of Bihar appeared and gave evidence along with representatives of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. The Madhya Pradesh Education Secretary arrived as scheduled, and the Committee decided to call the State again. Mr. Venugopal also asked the Speaker to act against the Social Welfare Secretaries of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, and Odisha.

All members of the PAC took note of the matter and the committee held that the absence amounts to breach of privilege, Mr. Venugopal said in the letter, urging the Speaker to take appropriate actions for the violation.

articles.title: Iran says resumption of war would not change its stances
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: To achieve peace and stability, the region must move towards complete absence of foreign forces, says Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday (October 25, 2026) that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's positions.

The remarks come amid mounting U.S and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran , as President Donald Trump said on Friday (October 23, 2026) that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the U.S-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on February 28 .

"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," said Mr. Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran.
"They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past," he added.

An April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the United States put an end to the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.
Iran has ‘lost complete control’ of Hormuz Strait: Rubio
Iran has detailed plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if war resumes, officials say
Iran says 7 oil tankers catch fire or damaged overnight in Strait of Hormuz

Iran has claimed control over Strait of Hormuz since the outbreak of the war and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt crossing without its authorisation, moves strongly opposed by Washington and countries in the region.
In response, the U.S has been maintaining a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.

In June, Iran agreed with the United States to a memorandum of understanding laying out a pathway to a permanent settlement of the conflict, only for the deal to later unravel as each side accused the other of violating it.
Tehran has since called for a return to the accord to end the conflict.

articles.title: Can the new fortified potato variety the Centre is promoting help with India’s hidden hunger problem?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Kufri Jamunia is a purple skinned and fleshed potato with higher levels of certain nutrients compared to regular potatoes. At present, however, taking into account its production costs, pricing, uptake in the market and its ability to deliver these nutrients, it is unclear if it can help with hidden hunger

Scientists at the ICAR-Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI) have developed a new potato variety called ‘kufri jamunia’ that has higher levels of anthocyanins, vitamin C, and certain micronutrients than regular potatoes. The Central government has been promoting it of late as a means to address hidden hunger, i.e. when people consume enough calories but still do not receive the necessary nutrients.

Usually, experts who fortify foods, focus on items like rice and iodised salt, which a large number of people in India consume, often throughout the year, thus ensuring the added nutrients are delivered to a significant chunk of the population. Kufri jamunia is however a potato, which people in India generally consume much less consistently than rice or salt, and the micronutrient intake depends on preparation methods and how the body absorbs them.

Kufri jamunia offers nutritional advantages, but they are substantial in some aspects more than others. Questions also linger about its ability to resist disease and retain nutrients through different Indian cooking methods.

The variety reportedly has a mealy texture. In one CPRI assessment involving 64 people, 95% rated its overall acceptability ‘good to excellent’ and 56% said its taste was very good. This study cohort, though, is too small to generalise the results. CPRI researchers themselves have proposed that kufri jamunia can be used in curries, parathas, soups, baked goods, and dehydrated flours.

Importantly, kufri jamunia potatoes also have purple skin and flesh, which could affect consumer interest. Research on other biofortified foods has already shown that while people are generally willing to pay modest premiums — the national average cost of ordinary potatoes purchased wholesale is around ₹17/kg — whether they accept a new variety depends on its appearance, their awareness, taste, and of course local preferences.

The CPRI team developed the kufri jamunia variety by crossing two potato lines, MS/8-1148 and CP4242, in 2015. MS/8-1148 is high in vitamin C whereas CP4242 had purple skin and flesh. The result, formally called MSP/16-307, could naturally accumulate higher concentrations of specific nutrients as it grew. The team then conducted trials, including multi-location testing, in 2021-2023.

Based on the trial data, the Central Sub-Committee on Crop Standards, Notification and Release of Varieties for Horticultural Crops approved the variety in mid-2024 and the government notified it in November that year. The variety’s plants produce 10-12 medium to large tubers each and mature in around 90 days. The purple colour comes from anthocyanins — organic compounds also found in jamun and blueberries.

According to the Press Information Bureau, 100 g of kufri jamunia flesh contains around 42.75 mg of vitamin C (versus 23.15 mg in regular potatoes), 42.05 mg of anthocyanins, 2.28 mg of zinc (versus 0.28 mg), 3.22 mg of iron (versus 0.57 mg), and 161 micrograms of carotenoids. And per the CPRI team’s findings themselves, published in Potato Journal in 2025, 100 g of kufri jamunia was found to have a range of carotenoid levels, from 15.6 micrograms in Kanpur to 298.4 micrograms in Raipur, during the multi-location trials. Kufri jamunia also contains slightly less zinc than kufri neelkanth and slightly less iron than kufri manik; the latter are other coloured potato varieties developed at the Institute.

Anthocyanins are known to have antioxidant properties, although whether the same benefits will accrue when delivered by kufri jamunia potatoes is not known. And in the absence of similar studies, the same caveat goes for iron and zinc.

A 2016 study in Food Chemistry examined purple-fleshed potatoes and reported that steaming and microwaving generally preserved more of the nutritional substances than stir-frying did. However, again, research specific to kufri jamunia is not available.
Nutrient availability and delivery constitutes one half of a biofortification programme; the other half is determined by cultivation.

At the Modipuram research station, according to the Potato Journal paper, the team recorded an average yield of 49.01 tonnes per hectare after three months, across three seasons, whereas subsequent multi-location trials, including at Modipuram, recorded an overall mean of 31.96 tonnes per hectare across north (36.77 tonnes), central (33.79 tonnes), and eastern (25.91 tonnes) India.

articles.title: Direct recruitment exam for land surveyors, VAOs goes off smoothly in Yadgir
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The written examination was conducted by the Karnataka Examinations Authority across 25 designated centres in the district

The direct recruitment examination for the posts of land surveyors and village administrative officers (VAO) in the Revenue Department passed off smoothly across 25 designated examination centres in Yadgir district on Sunday.
​The written examination was conducted by Karnataka Examinations Authority (KEA).
​Providing details on candidate turnout, Deputy Commissioner Rahul Pandve stated that out of the 9,607 registered candidates for the morning session, 6,918 appeared, while 2,689 skipped the test.
In the afternoon session, 6,572 candidates out of the 9,152 registered applicants turned up for the exam, while 2,580 candidates remained absent.

​The district administration ensured stringent security measures, strict protocols and full compliance with KEA guidelines to prevent any untoward incidents and to maintain the integrity of the examination process.
​Adequate police security was deployed across all 25 centres.
Basic facilities, including drinking water, uninterrupted power supply and emergency medical support, were arranged for the benefit of the candidates.

​Acknowledging the inter-departmental synergy, Mr. Pandve commended the coordinated efforts of the Police Department, the Department of Public Instruction, the Health Department, GESCOM and the KSRTC.

On behalf of the district administration, he expressed his appreciation for all officers, deputy chief superintendents, observers and staff for ensuring a transparent and seamless conduct of the examination.

articles.title: Nelakondapalli Buddhist site in Telangana to be developed as international heritage and tourism destination: Minister
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The historic Buddhist Stupa at Nelakondapalli and its surrounding areas in the Palair Assembly constituency of Khammam district will be developed into an international Buddhist heritage and tourism destination, informed Revenue, Housing and Information and Public Relations Minister Ponguleti Srinivas Reddy.
The Minister laid the foundation stone for tourism facilities and the restoration and conservation of the protected Buddhist site at Nelakondapalli on Monday.

Highlighting the ancient site’s rich heritage and historical significance, the Minister said excavations conducted there in the past had unearthed several antiquities, which were subsequently preserved at a museum in Hyderabad.

He said a meeting would be held at Nelakondapalli to seek the views and suggestions of Buddhist monks, experts and local people on transforming the ancient site into a major tourism destination while preserving its rich heritage for future generations.
Director of the Department of Heritage K. Arjun Rao and Khammam Collector Divakara T.S. were present.

articles.title: Andhra Pradesh braces for 11th very severe cyclonic storm
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Arnab could be the first VSCS to affect the State since Titli in 2018; IMD records 10 such storms between 1970 and 2023

Andhra Pradesh has experienced 61 cyclonic storms since 1970, but only a few have intensified into Very Severe Cyclonic Storms (VSCS). The State is now bracing for one such storm, Arnab, nearly eight years after Titli struck in October 2018.

According to the India Meteorological Department’s (IMD) records of cyclonic storms that affected the Andhra Pradesh coast between 1970 and 2023, the State witnessed 10 Very Severe Cyclonic Storms during the period. Arnab would be the 11th, if it reaches this intensity.

The IMD classifies cyclonic storms based on their maximum sustained wind speeds. A cyclonic storm has wind speeds of 62-88 kmph, a severe cyclonic storm 89-117 kmph, and a Very Severe Cyclonic Storm 118-167 kmph. An Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm has wind speeds of 168-221 kmph, while a Super Cyclonic Storm has wind speeds exceeding 221 kmph.

The 10 previous VSCS events occurred in 1999, 2000, 2011, 2013, 2014 and 2018. The year 2013 alone witnessed three such storms: Phailin in October, Lehar in November and Madi in December. In 2014, Hudhud caused extensive damage in Visakhapatnam, Vizianagaram, Srikakulam and East Godavari districts.

According to a case study by C. Hari Kiran of the Andhra Pradesh State Development Planning Society (APSDPS), Hudhud recorded wind speeds of 181.6 kmph. Phailin was even more intense, with wind speeds of 200-210 kmph. Weather models indicate that Arnab may be less intense, with its maximum wind speed expected to be around 140 kmph.
The last Very Severe Cyclonic Storm to affect the State, according to the IMD records, was Titli, which formed over the Bay of Bengal in October 2018 and made landfall near Palasa.
More recent cyclones, including Montha and Michaung, were classified as Severe Cyclonic Storms.

articles.title: BJP protests Kharge’s remark on PM’s father in Bihar and Jharkhand
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Party leaders stage marches in Patna and Ranchi; burn effigies of Congress president

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) units in Bihar and Jharkhand on Monday (October 26, 2026) staged protests against Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge over his controversial remark, “ Modi ka baap bhi jayega ” (Modi’s father will also be defeated), made at a party event in Patna. BJP leaders and workers in both States took out marches and burnt effigies of the Congress leader.

In Patna, hundreds of BJP workers, led by State unit president Sanjay Saraogi, took to the streets and raised slogans against Mr. Kharge. Before burning his effigy, some protesters slapped it to register their protest. They also carried placards and posters bearing slogans against Congress leader Rahul Gandhi.

The protesters gathered near the State BJP office and marched through the Income Tax roundabout to Dak Bungalow Chauraha, where they burnt an effigy of the Congress president. Several senior party leaders and office-bearers, including Cooperative Minister Ram Kripal Yadav and MLA and Chief Whip Sanjeev Chaurasia, participated in the protest.

Slamming the Congress, Mr. Saraogi said, “One may disagree with the Prime Minister’s politics, but the use of derogatory language regarding his late parents is unacceptable under any circumstances. This is not the first time indecent language has been used on the soil of Bihar concerning the Prime Minister’s late mother as well.”

He recalled that derogatory remarks against the Prime Minister’s mother had previously been made in his home district of Darbhanga. Mr. Saraogi said that remarks about a deceased family member violate political decorum, and the people of Bihar would not tolerate such language.

“The frustration felt by the Congress and the ‘ Mahagathbandhan ’ [Grand Alliance] leaders is due to rejection by the public. Instead of addressing issues of public concern from political platforms, Congress leaders are showing their frustration through inappropriate and undignified remarks,” Mr. Saraogi said.

articles.title: H.K. Patil sees need for setting up irrigation study centre to honour V.V. Deshpande
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The former Irrigation Minister says such a centre will take up research and extension activities in North Karnataka

There is a need to set up an irrigation study centre in the name of irrigation expert Vithalrao Vaikunthrao Deshpande either in the Visvesvaraya Technological University (VTU), Belagavi, or the Karnatak University, Dharwad, the former Irrigation Minister H.K. Patil said in Dharwad on Sunday.
Mr. Patil called for the establishment of the centre that will take up research and extension activities in North Karnataka.
“It should be named after Deshpande to honour his outstanding contributions to the development of irrigation in the State,” he said.
“A study centre in his name will help preserve his achievements and inspire future generations of engineers,” he said.
He was speaking at the birth centenary celebration of the late V.V. Deshpande, organised in collaboration with various engineers associations at Alur Venkatrao Bhavan there.

Deshpande who belonged to Haliyal in Uttar Kannada had played a significant role in several major irrigation projects, including the Ghataprabha, the Malaprabha, the Bhadra and the Kali. “However, despite his exceptional engineering contributions, we have failed in adequately recognising his services,” he said.
He admitted that even during his tenure as Water Resources Minister, sufficient efforts were not made to honour Deshpande’s legacy.

“I have seen that officials who had worked with him fondly referred to him as Annadata. Beyond his engineering expertise, Deshpande empowered farmers by helping create irrigation infrastructure essential for agricultural prosperity. However, he did not receive the recognition he deserved from the administration and society,” he said.
He thanked the organisers for celebrating Deshpande’s birth centenary.
On behalf of the Deshpande family, the Lifetime Achievement Award was presented to retired engineer M.B. Parappagowda, while Jagadish Nandi received the Award for Excellence in Civil Engineering.
MLA Arvind Bellad, who felicitated the award winners, praised Rajan Deshpande for honouring his father’s legacy through the awards and encouraging professionals in the field of engineering.
Mr. Bellad observed that standards of integrity and excellence in society, administration and politics have declined over the years.

articles.title: MSMEs seek improvement of electricity infrastructure in Coimbatore district
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Tamil Nadu Association of Cottage and Tiny Enterprises, representing micro industries in Coimbatore city, has appealed to the Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited to strengthen the electricity infrastructure in Coimbatore district.

Its president J. James said in a press release on Monday that given the high concentration of small-scale industrial units alongside residential areas in the district, additional dedicated 11 kV/22 kV power lines should be connected to all 110 kV substations to prevent power outages during the summer season. The power lines established for this purpose should not exceed a maximum length of five km as currently, some extend up to approximately 12 km.

In Coimbatore city and surrounding town panchayats and panchayats, new, high-capacity, and high-quality transformers should be erected to address voltage fluctuations. All power lines and sub-stations should be inter-connected to allow flexible routing. In the event of a fault, the affected section should be isolated while ensuring an uninterrupted power supply to the remaining areas.

The Ring Main Units (RMUs) and automatic switches installed by the Energy Department in the district require better maintenance. ‘Fault Off-Call’ (FOC) service specifically for addressing night hour power outages should be established in all areas and circles surrounding Coimbatore city.

In Tamil Nadu, there are over one lakh LTCT (Low Tension Current Transformer) electricity connections, supporting more than 10 lakh micro and small-scale entrepreneurs. Since September 2023, the fixed charge (demand charge) has been increased from ₹35 per kilowatt to ₹162 per kilowatt. On July 29, 2026, the Association representatives submitted a memorandum to the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu requesting that the fixed charge be reverted to the previous rate of ₹35 per kilowatt (for a sanctioned load of up to 112 kW). Although the Chief Minister assured us that action would be taken, this has not yet been implemented. In the interest of the welfare of micro and small-scale entrepreneurs, the demand charges should be reduced for the LT CT industries.

The conductors of existing High Tension (HT) power lines must be upgraded to ensure the entire line can withstand maximum current loads. Further, the capacity of existing distribution transformers should be increased to facilitate higher power distribution.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence giant Anthropic files for Initial Public Offering
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: The filing sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the SpaceX initial public offering in June that raised a record $86 billion

Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers on Monday (October 26, 2026) for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever, even as its top executive warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

The filing sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the SpaceX initial public offering in June that raised a record $86 billion. An Anthropic IPO would also put the company ahead of OpenAI in going public in what is expected to be a pair of blockbuster stock debuts for the rival AI labs.

The filing comes weeks after CEO Dario Amodei argued in an essay for slowing the development of the most advanced AI models. An IPO could provide Anthropic with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion. The amount the company ultimately raises remains uncertain, as do its final valuation and offering price, but even at lower estimates, it would turn the five-year-old startup into one of the world's most valuable companies and potentially boost the wealth of Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela, by billions of dollars.

The 335-page document showed Anthropic's revenue is growing rapidly, but like many other tech companies going public, it has yet to turn a profit. The company behind the chatbot Claude reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026. That compares to a loss of $13 billion in the same period a year earlier.

Despite the losses, Anthropic, valued earlier this year at $965 billion by private investors, is reportedly set to see that value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established. At $1.5 trillion, Anthropic would rank among the world's most valuable public companies, alongside Tesla.
As for money raised, the offering could raise as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the current record set by another one of Musk's companies, SpaceX, earlier this year.
In a regulatory filing, Anthropic said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol "ANT."
In the filing, the company said it could use some of that money on acquiring other businesses and technology as well as investing in infrastructure to grow its business to take on rivals.
Formed in 2021 by ex-OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company and the two leaders, Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, are widely seen as bitter rivals.

But they have plenty of other competitors, including Google, newer startups in the U.S. and China and Musk's SpaceX, which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI division have all been losing more money than they make because of the huge costs in resources in building AI, fueling concerns of a bubble.

The IPO would help cover any cash shortfall as well as shower extraordinary wealth on Anthropic's seven founders, including Amodei and his sister. Collectively they own nearly 500 million shares, though it's unclear from the offering document how much that will represent of the company after the IPO.

The filing also listed a host of risks for the San Francisco-based Anthropic, ranging from not being able to retain key staff, navigate regulatory roadblocks and secure enough compute power to run its AI systems.

articles.title: UN-commissioned experts say Gaza ceasefire has not stopped Israel from committing genocide
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: The findings by the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory could be used by prosecutors at the International Criminal Court or in other jurisdictions to try to bring justice to victims and their relatives

A ceasefire agreement in Gaza has not stopped what a group of independent experts commissioned by the UN say is genocide carried out by Israel in the territory, the team said in a new report on Monday (October 26, 2026). They also accused Israeli forces of crimes against humanity, including torture and rape, in the West Bank.
Israel, which denies both the genocide and the sexual assault claims, did not immediately respond to the report's publication.

articles.title: Protests in France | Beginning of the end of Macronism
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: A student protest over deteriorating school conditions has snowballed into a nationwide movement, fuelled by a cost-of-living crisis and sluggish growth, putting mounting pressure on Emmanuel Macron’s centrist administration

France is in turmoil. More than half a million people hit the streets on October 17, as protests swept across the country. As the administration greeted the protesters with a large deployment of riot police, peaceful demonstrations were engulfed by violence in many places. Arsonists set fire to the Lyon tourist office and burnt down the Limoges City Hall, a historic municipal building. Protesters stormed the townhall in Marseille and attacked the prefect’s residence in Bordeaux. In Paris’s Place de la Republique, protesting youth who clashed with the police torched vehicles and looted shops. Luxury retailers such as Louis Vuitton, Hermes, Dior and Galeries Lafayette suffered millions of dollars in losses as their stores were ransacked. Police arrested or detained more than 6,000 people, including hundreds of minors.

With the police outnumbered and unable to protect public and private property, several cities resorted to full or partial curfews. Government officials have blamed the unrest on “seditionists from far-left fringe groups”. They have accused La France Insoumise, or LFI (France Unbowed), the leftwing political party launched by veteran politician Jean-Luc Melenchon (75), of inciting the protests with the aim of extracting political mileage ahead of the presidential elections in April 2027.

articles.title: U.K. PM Burnham backs principle of ‘earned settlement’ in immigration rules
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: An increase in the baseline qualifying period for settlement, from 5 of 15 years had been proposed by U.K. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood as part of a draft “earned settlement” immigration overhaul last year, during the Keir Starmer administration

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that he stands by the principle that settlement (permanent residence) in the U.K. should be “earned” and not granted automatically. An increase in the baseline qualifying period for settlement, from 5 of 15 years had been proposed by U.K. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood as part of a draft “earned settlement” immigration overhaul last year, during the Keir Starmer administration. Individuals could qualify for shorter or longer periods depending on income, immigration violations and other factors.

Indian citizens are likely to be significantly impacted by the new rules. Indian nationals constituted the largest group from outside the EU + (EU and a few other European countries) area to migrate long-term to the U.K. for the year ending December 2025.

“We’ll set out the plan on that quite soon,” Mr. Burnham said during a TV interview on Monday (October 26, 2026) morning. He said the government was still considering the responses received in the public consultation process that took place earlier this year. In recent weeks the Prime Minister has indicated that the government would soften the proposed stance towards social care workers. These individuals formed a significant part of the ‘Boriswave’ of migration – a surge in migrants in the early 2020s - who are now becoming eligible for settlement.

Mr. Burnham said that since the U.K. left the E.U. in 2016, things had not “played out as people said it would at the time” with the country’s economy weakening and control over immigration becoming more challenging. He said “revolving-door immigration” was being replaced by permanent immigration to the U.K.
Over the weekend, the Sunday Times had reported that Mr. Burnham had told the publication that he would be open to considering ‘free movement’ (i.e., right to live and work) between the U.K. and E.U.
In his Monday (October 26, 2026) interview, Mr. Burnham reiterated his wish to see the U.K. rejoin the E.U. in his lifetime, adding, however, that would “not move ahead of the public”.

“The British public …will be the bosses here. They will decide what will happen in relation to Brexit,” he said, as he denied that he was “testing the waters” with the public and media on how a return to the E.U. would be received.
The U.K. and EU are working towards concluding an agreement that would cover agriculture and immigration among other areas, at a summit meeting on November 20.
Mr. Burnham ruled out an early general election. The current parliament expires in 2029.

articles.title: Why West Bengal’s C-Sections, at nearly 1 in 2 births, demand a hard look
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: NFHS-6 data puts the rate of Caesarean sections in West Bengal at 44.5%, nearly double the 2015-16 level and significantly higher than the national average of 27.2%. Private facilities handle about 3 in 10 births but perform almost 6 in 10 of the operations

On September 29, 2015, a memo went out from Swasthya Bhawan, the West Bengal Health Department’s headquarters in Salt Lake, to every medical college principal and every district’s chief medical officer of health. Its subject was a concern the Union Health Ministry had raised about rising Caesarean sections rates, especially where the operation was not medically needed.

The memo enclosed a statement the World Health Organization (WHO) had issued that April. It suggested that chief medical officers, who license private clinics, carry out periodic “prescription audits” of Caesareans in private and government facilities.

At the time, the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-4, 2015-16) had found that about one in four births were Caesareans in West Bengal (23.8%). The latest sixth round (NFHS-6, 2023-24) puts the figure at 44.5%, close to double that level, against 27.2% for India. In Kolkata and North 24 Parganas it was found to be 67.5%, meaning about two of every three babies were born via a C-section.

A Caesarean section saves mothers and babies when labour goes wrong. It is also, however, major abdominal surgery, with slower recovery rates and higher risks of infection and bleeding, and it leaves a scar that can complicate later pregnancies.

The WHO statement said that across a population, Caesarean rates above 10% are not associated with fewer deaths of mothers or newborns. While the WHO does not recommend a specific rate , the increasing numbers of Caesarean births in West Bengal, and more widely in India, deserve attention.
The NFHS’s first three rounds, from 1992-93 to 2005-06, found West Bengal close to the national average when it came to C-sections, at 10.2% against 8.5% by the third NFHS round.

The State then pulled away. Its rate reached 32.6% in NFHS-5, for which West Bengal was surveyed in 2019-21, and by NFHS-6 (2023-24) the gap with India had widened from 1.7 percentage points in 2005-06 to 17.3.
The climb has also grown steeper. The rise of 13.6 points between 2005-06 and 2015-16 took a decade, while the latest 11.9 points came in four to five years.
The data cannot reveal how many of West Bengal’s operations were necessary, though it does show when and where the rise happened.

Of every 10 women who give birth in a private facility in West Bengal, 9 nine now have a C-section (87.7%). In 2015-16, the year of the memo, the figure was 70.9%. West Bengal’s numbers are also significantly higher than current the national private-sector rate, 54.1%.

While numbers in the government sector are lower, they are also on the rise: government facilities performed C-sections in 28.8% of the births they handled, up from 18.8% in 2015-16 and 1.7 times the national public-sector figure of 16.9%. In Kolkata, the share of births in government facilities delivered by C-section rose from 32.4% in NFHS-5 to 59.1% in NFHS-6.
Births are also increasingly moving to private facilities. Between NFHS-5 and NFHS-6 their share of the total rose from about 19% to about 29%, even as the public share fell from 72.4% to 65.8%.

Its subject was a concern the Union Health Ministry had raised about rising Caesarean sections rates, especially where the operation was not medically needed.

The memo enclosed a statement the World Health Organization (WHO) had issued that April. It suggested that chief medical officers, who license private clinics, carry out periodic “prescription audits” of Caesareans in private and government facilities.

At the time, the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-4, 2015-16) had found that about one in four births were Caesareans in West Bengal (23.8%). The latest sixth round (NFHS-6, 2023-24) puts the figure at 44.5%, close to double that level, against 27.2% for India. In Kolkata and North 24 Parganas it was found to be 67.5%, meaning about two of every three babies were born via a C-section.

A Caesarean section saves mothers and babies when labour goes wrong. It is also, however, major abdominal surgery, with slower recovery rates and higher risks of infection and bleeding, and it leaves a scar that can complicate later pregnancies.

The WHO statement said that across a population, Caesarean rates above 10% are not associated with fewer deaths of mothers or newborns. While the WHO does not recommend a specific rate , the increasing numbers of Caesarean births in West Bengal, and more widely in India, deserve attention.

The NFHS’s first three rounds, from 1992-93 to 2005-06, found West Bengal close to the national average when it came to C-sections, at 10.2% against 8.5% by the third NFHS round.

The State then pulled away. Its rate reached 32.6% in NFHS-5, for which West Bengal was surveyed in 2019-21, and by NFHS-6 (2023-24) the gap with India had widened from 1.7 percentage points in 2005-06 to 17.3.

The climb has also grown steeper. The rise of 13.6 points between 2005-06 and 2015-16 took a decade, while the latest 11.9 points came in four to five years.

The data cannot reveal how many of West Bengal’s operations were necessary, though it does show when and where the rise happened.

Of every 10 women who give birth in a private facility in West Bengal, 9 nine now have a C-section (87.7%). In 2015-16, the year of the memo, the figure was 70.9%. West Bengal’s numbers are also significantly higher than current the national private-sector rate, 54.1%.

While numbers in the government sector are lower, they are also on the rise: government facilities performed C-sections in 28.8% of the births they handled, up from 18.8% in 2015-16 and 1.7 times the national public-sector figure of 16.9%. In Kolkata, the share of births in government facilities delivered by C-section rose from 32.4% in NFHS-5 to 59.1% in NFHS-6.

Births are also increasingly moving to private facilities. Between NFHS-5 and NFHS-6 their share of the total rose from about 19% to about 29%, even as the public share fell from 72.4% to 65.8%.

articles.title: Amgen drug combined with immunotherapy extends survival in lung cancer trial
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The Amgen drug is currently approved for adults in the advanced stages of small cell lung cancer that has worsened despite chemotherapy, based on data showing that Imdelltra reduced the risk of death by 40%

Amgen's Imdelltra used in combination with ​AstraZeneca's immunotherapy Imfinzi reduced the risk of death by 58% compared ⁠to the Astra drug alone in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, according to data from a study presented at a major medical meeting on Saturday.
Imfinzi is currently the standard of care following chemotherapy ‌for patients with this very aggressive and hard-to-treat disease whose cancer does not worsen after initial chemotherapy.
The study found that those given both drugs ‌lived for a median of 21.1 months, compared with 12.7 months for those treated only ‌with ⁠Imfinzi.

"If you give Imdelltra earlier and earlier, you get bigger clinical benefit," ⁠said Paul Burton, chief medical officer at California-based Amgen. He called the results "unprecedented in advancing the treatment of extensive-stage small cell lung cancer."
Imdelltra's U.S. list price is about $30,000 per cycle, or over $390,000 a year. Wall Street analysts ​have estimated annual sales reaching more ‌than $2.5 billion by 2030, according to LSEG data.

The Amgen drug is currently approved for adults in the advanced stages of small cell lung cancer that has worsened despite chemotherapy, based on data showing that Imdelltra reduced the risk of death by 40%.

Full results ‌of the 563-patient trial were presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology ​meeting in Madrid and published in the New England Journal of Medicine . Amgen had previously announced that the Phase 3 study was successful.

Imdelltra ⁠belongs to a dual-target class of drugs called bispecific antibodies designed to pull immune system T cells into contact with cancer cells to destroy them. Imfinzi is an older type of ‌immunotherapy that essentially blocks the mechanism tumors use to hide from immune-system assault.

Most lung cancer cases are non-small cell, while up to 15% are the small cell variety targeted by Imdelltra. About 250,000 new cases are diagnosed worldwide each year, according to the U.S. National Institutes of Health.
Very few people diagnosed with small cell lung cancer are candidates for surgery, and most are initially given radiotherapy and chemotherapy, Burton said.
Survival rates depend on ‌when the cancer is diagnosed, but the overall 5-year rate is only around 9%, according to the American ​Cancer Society.
Amgen said that nearly 80% of trial patients treated with the combination were alive after one year, compared with 53% of those on Imfinzi ⁠alone, as patient follow-up continues.

articles.title: IIT Bombay develops low-cost device to screen for anaemia, sickle cell disease
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The researchers said their patented automated smearing device can be manufactured cost-effectively and the test itself requires only a pipette, glass slides, an inexpensive chemical, vials for the sickling treatment, and a ruler or imaging device to measure smear length
The Indian Institute of Technology Bombay on Friday said its researchers have developed a low-cost device that can screen for anaemia and sickle cell disease using a drop of blood.

A research team from the Department of Chemical Engineering, led by Mahesh Tirumkudulu, has developed a simple, low-cost point-of-care approach that uses the length of a blood smear (the distance that a drop of blood spreads across a glass slide) to detect anaemia, and detect and monitor treatment for sickle cell disease. IIT Bombay said.

Prof Tirumkudulu's team built their own automated device to have a uniform method of creating a smear. Under these controlled conditions, the researchers observed that blood from different people gives different smear lengths, and this difference holds useful information.
Prof. Tirumkudulu explained that more viscous blood spreads less easily and, therefore, produces a shorter and thicker smear under the same conditions.

Once the team confirmed that the method could sense small differences in blood viscosity, they decided to investigate whether those differences could help identify disease. It was found that anaemia lowers red blood cell concentration and haemoglobin, while sickle cell disease makes red blood cells rigid.

The researchers said their patented automated smearing device can be manufactured cost-effectively. Also, the test itself requires only a pipette, glass slides, an inexpensive chemical, vials for the sickling treatment, and a ruler or imaging device to measure smear length, they added.

"This makes our technique particularly useful in places where conventional diagnostic laboratories are difficult to access, and it doesn't require any special expertise to use," said Dr. Mahrukh Mir, a former PhD scholar in Prof Tirumkudulu's lab, and the first author of the study.
The researchers pointed out that blood viscosity cutoffs vary for various groups of people because certain genetic differences affect how blood reacts when oxygen levels drop.

Also, the anaemia test could miss identifying some patients when the usual link between viscosity and anaemia does not hold, such as in a rare condition called hyperviscosity syndrome, where blood plasma is unusually thick.

Currently, the technology is licensed to Rheoheme Private Limited, an IIT Bombay startup, and the team is now working with the National Institute for Research in Tribal Health, Jabalpur, in Madhya Pradesh and All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) Nagpur, toward regulatory approval, while exploring extending the device to measure clotting time and glucose levels.
"Our initial aim was to understand the physics of spreading blood drop, and that led to the medical applications," added Prof Tirumkudulu.

articles.title: Most people globally face 'high genetic risk' for three common diseases: Study
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The team analysed data from two major population biobanks that include whole genome sequencing, covering nearly one million individuals

Most people worldwide could be categorised as having a high genetic risk for three of 28 common conditions, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease and schizophrenia, even if they might not develop them, a new study has found.

Researchers, led by the UK's University of Exeter, described the 'average' human genome, finding that everyone, regardless of their current health status, could be considered at risk for numerous conditions based on their genetics alone.

Every person's genome, or the average human genome, contains around five million variants, or DNA locations that differ between individuals, the findings published in the journal Genome Medicine reveal.

The locations include around 10,000 variants that alter gene sequences, which can have positive or negative effect, ranging from lactose intolerance to drug response, though are often biologically neutral, they show.

Each person also carries between one and three rare variants previously shown to cause serious genetic diseases, and another 50 rare variants that are currently of uncertain clinical relevance, the researchers found.
The team analysed data from two major population biobanks -- the UK Biobank and the US' All of Us -- that include whole genome sequencing, covering nearly one million individuals.

Senior author Caroline Wright, from the University of Exeter, said, "Whole genome sequencing has become such an important tool in diagnosing genetic disease, and we're increasingly moving towards genetic screening for predicting disease."

"Yet most people are unaware of just how much genetic variation is present in every genome. Actually, variation is the norm. For the first time, our study outlines what to expect in the average human genome, which can benefit clinicians and patients across the word in understanding, interpreting and contextualising genomics," Wright said.
The researchers also analysed numerous polygenic risk scores, which consider all known genetic factors to calculate a person's future risk of developing a disease.

"... applying polygenic scores (PGS) for 28 common diseases within UKB (UK Biobank), we estimate that the average person is in the top 10 per cent for (nearly) three conditions, and around one in five people are in the top one per cent for at least one PGS," the authors wrote.
"Importantly, we found that everyone carries a small number of genetic variants linked to disease, although many of these will not actually cause disease in that individual," Wright said.

The senior author added, "It is therefore crucial to consider context when interpreting findings from genetic testing, including symptoms or family history of disease as well as other clinical and environmental risk factors. Our findings also provide important context for professionals who are interpreting genetic testing results or commissioning genetic screening programmes."

articles.title: Bengaluru’s BMTC drivers, traffic police, pourakarmikas, construction workers show reduced lung function: Survey
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: A three-year long study in Bengaluru of over 10,000 frontline workers has brought to light reduced lung function among BMTC bus drivers, traffic police, pourakarmikas and construction workers — sections most exposed to polluted air.

The study, done by the VAAYU Occupational & Environmental Respiratory Illness Clinic (VOERIC), screened 4,517 BMTC drivers, 3,285 traffic police personnel, 2,169 construction workers and 379 pourakarmikas.
A traffic policeman wears a mask at a traffic signal in Bengaluru. | Photo Credit: BHAGYA PRAKASH
All the groups that were screened showed higher-than-normal prevalence of early lung-function abnormalities.

Among the occupations, pourakarmikas were found to have the highest proportion of workers with the PRISm pattern, an indication of reduced lung capacity. Around 45% of them showed indications of reduced lung function.
BMTC workers and traffic police followed, with 29.5% and 28%, respectively, showing reduced lung function. Among construction workers, 15% showed a PRISm pattern.
Around 2.6% of BMTC drivers, 2.3% pourakarmikas, 2.1% construction workers, and 1% traffic police personnel reported signs of obstructive airflow.
The survey also found that 88.2% of the BMTC drivers never used a mask, as was the case with 55% traffic police, 37.9% construction workers, and 16.3% pourakarmikas.
Workers breaking stones during pipeline work at Race Course in Bengaluru. | Photo Credit: SUDHAKARA JAIN
The subjects were also analysed for comorbidities, and the results revealed a grim situation, with high levels of obesity reported among the sections.
Pourakarmikas had the highest proportion at 62%, closely followed by BMTC drivers, 60.7% of whom were found to be obese/overweight. For traffic police, the figure stood at 51.3%.
The figures are much higher than the India reference figure of 28.6%.

A traffic policeman wears a mask at a traffic signal in Bengaluru. | Photo Credit: BHAGYA PRAKASH

All the groups that were screened showed higher-than-normal prevalence of early lung-function abnormalities.

Among the occupations, pourakarmikas were found to have the highest proportion of workers with the PRISm pattern, an indication of reduced lung capacity. Around 45% of them showed indications of reduced lung function.

BMTC workers and traffic police followed, with 29.5% and 28%, respectively, showing reduced lung function. Among construction workers, 15% showed a PRISm pattern.

Around 2.6% of BMTC drivers, 2.3% pourakarmikas, 2.1% construction workers, and 1% traffic police personnel reported signs of obstructive airflow.

The survey also found that 88.2% of the BMTC drivers never used a mask, as was the case with 55% traffic police, 37.9% construction workers, and 16.3% pourakarmikas.

Pourakarmikas had the highest proportion at 62%, closely followed by BMTC drivers, 60.7% of whom were found to be obese/overweight. For traffic police, the figure stood at 51.3%.

The figures are much higher than the India reference figure of 28.6%.

articles.title: Gujarat govt. declares Devbhoomi Dwarka, Kutch, Jamnagar and Porbandar as drought-affected
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel said the decision on drought declaration was taken as per the guidelines of the Centre after monsoon ended in the state; as per the Centre's 2016 guideline on drought, the announcement will be in effect for six months, Mr. Patel added.
The Gujarat government on Monday (October 26, 2026) declared Devbhoomi Dwarka, Kutch, Jamnagar and Porbandar districts as drought-affected.

Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel said the decision on drought declaration was taken as per the guidelines of the Centre after monsoon ended in the state. As per the Centre's 2016 guideline on drought, the announcement will be in effect for six months, Mr. Patel added.

"The state has received 89% rain this monsoon. However, Devbhoomi Dwarka, Kutch, Jamnagar and Porbandar received very little rain. So these four districts have been declared drought-affected," Mr. Patel told reporters.
The State government will stand with farmers during these difficult times, he added.

"The state government will give assistance under SDRF (State Disaster Response Fund) of ₹8,500 per hectare for two hectares to farmers whose crops have failed. The state government has already started providing fodder at discounted rates of ₹2 per kilo," Mr. Patel said.

"The Gujarat government will provide ₹80 per cattle to cattle shelters for upkeep of the animals. It will also provide 150 days of employment under VB-G RAM G (Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar & Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) ) in affected districts. This will be implemented from November 1," Mr. Patel said.
The state government, under the guidance of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, will always remain with farmers and people and take decisions in their favour, Mr. Patel asserted.

articles.title: Peace for progress: on the SCO, regional cooperation, the fight against terror
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Economic objectives can be met only in a stable security environment

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh’s address at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Tajikistan, on Tuesday marks another significant occasion since Operation Sindoor (2025) when India has used the multilateral forum to raise the issue of terrorism, including cross-border terrorism from Pakistan. He said that regional cooperation cannot be meaningful if countries approached terrorism selectively. Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar’s presence added significance to the remarks, underscoring New Delhi’s diplomatic challenge within an organisation whose members have divergent strategic interests and security priorities. India has consistently argued that terrorism cannot be divorced from the broader agenda of regional peace, economic integration and development. By calling on SCO member-states to dismantle the ecosystem of terrorism, he reiterated that the threat must be addressed at its source rather than treated as an isolated security challenge. The intervention follows India’s refusal to endorse the joint statement at the 2025 SCO Defence Ministers’ meet in Qingdao, China. New Delhi had objected to a draft that failed to reflect its concerns over cross-border and Pakistan-sponsored terrorism, including the Pahalgam attack (2025), while referring to militant activities in Balochistan. India maintained that such an approach would undermine the organisation’s credibility by overlooking the threat it had brought before its members.

The SCO has the potential to advance regional stability, trade and connectivity instead of becoming another source of strategic friction. Yet, its effectiveness will remain limited if political disagreements prevent members from developing a common approach to security threats. India’s position is not that cooperation on trade, culture, connectivity and development must be suspended until every security dispute is resolved. Rather, these objectives cannot be met independently of a stable security environment. Economic corridors require predictable borders, investors need confidence in the rule of law, and transport networks must be violence- and disruption-free. Connectivity projects such as the International North-South Transport Corridor and the development of Chabahar Port offer Central Asia connectivity with wider markets. Their long-term value, however, depends on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, alongside conditions that allow goods, capital and people to move freely. The SCO’s challenge is to translate its stated commitment to combating terrorism into practical cooperation through intelligence-sharing, action against terror financing, disruption of recruitment networks and the denial of safe havens to terrorist groups. While retaining its principle against terrorism, India should lead efforts to achieve more regional cooperation in tackling it.

articles.title: Bitter and sweet: on FSSAI draft restrictions, added sugars in infant foods
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The FSSAI must expand restrictions to cover all added sugars in infant foods

The Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2020 currently allow manufacturers to add sucrose and fructose, provided their combined total does not exceed 20% of the carbohydrates in a product intended for infants aged 0-6 months. In a draft proposal, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has pitched to eliminate this allowance — in line with WHO’s recommendation to have infants breastfeed exclusively for the first six months, followed by nutritionally adequate complementary foods avoiding added sugars until 24 months. While corporations have defended sugary formulations as abiding by the Codex Alimentarius, public health experts have repeatedly described their decision to sell infant foods with added sugar as nutritional dumping. Adding sugar has often been a commercial strategy, as it serves as a cheap bulking agent, improves palatability and encourages repeat purchases. WHO’s nutrient and promotion profile model for baby foods in 2022 also identified sweet purées and products in which fruits released sugars during processing as concerns. While the FSSAI’s draft proposal is a step in the right direction, stopping here would allow manufacturers to replace sucrose with another sweetening ingredient. It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.

articles.title: NDA secures six of nine urban local bodies in Kadapa district unopposed
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes

articles.title: Owner, mahout booked for neglected elephant in Kozhikode
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Forest officials find signs of severe malnutrition and chain-related injuries during an inspection at Ekarool near Unnikulam
The Forest department has registered a case against the owner and mahout of an elephant, Cheriyaparambath Gopalan, for allegedly failing to provide the animal with adequate food and care.
The action followed an inspection by a team of forest officials and veterinary doctors at the owner’s residence in Ekarool near Unnikulam in Kozhikode district.
Blood samples collected from the elephant were sent to Pookode Veterinary College for analysis. The report indicated severe malnutrition and inadequate care.

During the inspection, officials found that the elephant was not being fed the prescribed diet recorded in its care register. The inadequate feeding had left the animal severely weakened, they said. Injuries and sores caused by chains rubbing against its legs were also found.

There were allegations that the elephant had been used for timber-hauling work despite its poor health.The elephant was placed under the care of social forestry officials and veterinary doctors, who are overseeing its feeding and treatmen.

The owner, meanwhile, said the elephant had been receiving treatment from a doctor in Thrissur because of its weakness. He claimed that it had last been taken to a temple procession during the previous Thrissur Pooram and had not been used for timber hauling or other strenuous work in recent months.
